newsitem.title: USA: EMU success hinges on structural reform - Chase.
newsitem.headline: EMU success hinges on structural reform - Chase.

text.p: Risks of a delay in Europe's planned single currency project are slim, but the possibility of a post-1999 collapse in the system exists if structural reform is not undertaken, economists at Chase Manhattan Bank told clients on Monday.

"The real threat to the project is not that it (fails to) start on time, since I think they have gone too far down the road to call it off," said Robin Marshall, head of European economic research at the bank.
"But there is a non-negligible risk that the project disintegrates if there isn't more structural reform in the EU economy."
Working in EMU's favor, Marshall said, was a state of relative equilibrium in inflation and real exchange rates within the European Union.
He also noted that, apart from Ireland and the UK, the economies of key EU member states were fairly cyclically synchronized.
Conversely, Marshall said that high levels of unemployment within Europe posed a major risk to the system.
"Unemployment is at very high levels and obviously that does tend to cause political strains ... and increase the odds of a peasant revolt."
Marshall, based in Chase's London office, spoke along with New York-based chief economist John Lipsky at a panel discussion on EMU and the euro intended for Chase clients.
The economists said that the EMU project's timetable was acting as a necessary weapon in the fight against "Euro-sclerosis."
"I think that the success of EMU as a fulcrum for policy change is a critical element in determining the fate of the EMU process," said Lipsky.
